summary: Describes version 3 of the Network File System protocol, so that people can write compatible implementations. It is an informational description, not an Internet standard.

eli5.summary: A way for one computer to use files stored on another as if they were on its own. This is the third edition of the instructions.

questions: what is the difference between nfs v2 and v3
subtitle: How Sun's third-generation network file system lets one machine use another's files, with safer, faster writes.

tldr.problem: NFS version 2 could not handle large files, forced every write to disk before replying, and needed many extra calls just to check file attributes.
tldr.mechanism: NFS version 3 keeps the stateless RPC design but adds 64-bit sizes and offsets, attributes returned on most replies, a server-side ACCESS check, and unsafe writes that a later COMMIT call makes durable.
tldr.outcome: The document is Informational and was written so people can build compatible implementations. The IETF was not involved in creating or maintaining it.

today: RFC 1813 is an Informational document, not an Internet standard, and the metadata records no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It describes version 3 as defined at the time it was published, June 1995.

sections.title: What NFS Version 3 Covers
sections.content:
RFC 1813 describes NFS version 3, Sun's protocol for transparent remote access to shared file systems across networks. It is built on Remote Procedure Call (RPC) and the External Data Representation (XDR), which makes it independent of machine, operating system, network architecture and transport protocol. The initial version is described in RFC 1094.

The document covers three pieces. The NFS version 3 protocol itself, the supporting MOUNT protocol (which lets clients attach remote directory trees and lets servers grant access to a restricted set of clients), and a short description of how the Network Lock Manager (NLM) changes between version 3 and version 4.

The RFC says the normative text is the description of the RPC procedures, their arguments and results. The material on implementation practice is explanation only and does not carry the same authority.

An IESG note states that the IETF is not involved in creating or maintaining this specification. That is why it is not on the standards track.
sections.eli5: NFS is like a shared filing cabinet in another room that you can open from your desk. This document is the instruction book so that anyone can build a compatible cabinet and desk.

sections.title: Stateless Servers and Smart Clients
sections.content:
The protocol assumes a stateless server: the server does not need to remember anything about its clients to work correctly. After a crash, the client just keeps retrying a request until the server answers, and does not even need to know the server went down.

The RFC puts the division of labor bluntly: NFS servers are dumb and NFS clients are smart. If a server cannot support an operation, it may return NFS3ERR_NOTSUP, and the client is expected to recover. A server may still keep non-critical state, such as read-ahead data in a cache, as long as losing it is harmless.

Pathnames are resolved one segment at a time by the LOOKUP procedure, and the client builds the hierarchical name space using mounts. Most data-modifying procedures are synchronous: when they return, the data is on stable storage.

The service runs over RPC as program 100003, version 3, normally over TCP and UDP on port 2049. Permissions are checked from the RPC credentials on every call, using flavors such as AUTH_UNIX, AUTH_DES or AUTH_KERB.
sections.eli5: The server is like a librarian who forgets everyone the moment they leave the desk. That is fine, because each person brings a note saying exactly what they want, and asks again if there is no answer.

sections.title: Changes from Version 2
sections.content:
Version 3 addresses new requirements. Bigger files and file systems needed 64-bit file sizes and offsets, and the size and fileid attributes were widened to eight-byte unsigned integers. File handles became variable length, up to 64 bytes, instead of a fixed 32 bytes. Limits on transfer sizes and on filename lengths were relaxed; the transfer sizes are reported by FSINFO.

To cut network traffic, procedures that change attributes can return the new attributes, and operations that modify a directory return its old and new attributes. The new ACCESS procedure lets the server do the permission check, which fixes surprising permission errors caused by mapping the superuser ID.

The ROOT and WRITECACHE procedures were removed. New ones were added: MKNOD for special files, READDIRPLUS for directory entries with handles and attributes, FSSTAT and FSINFO for dynamic and static file system information, PATHCONF for POSIX data, and COMMIT for asynchronous writes. Procedures are numbered 0 (NULL) to 21 (COMMIT).
sections.eli5: Version 3 is the same cabinet with bigger drawers, a longer label for each folder, and a few new helpers so you do not have to ask as many questions.

sections.title: Safe Asynchronous Writes
sections.content:
In version 2 every write had to reach stable storage before the server replied, which limited write throughput. Version 3 lets a client send a WRITE with the stable field set to UNSTABLE, meaning the server may reply before the data is safely on disk. The client later sends COMMIT to flush the data, much like the POSIX fsync call.

The reply to a write says how safe the data is through its committed field. If the client asked for FILE_SYNC, the server must answer FILE_SYNC; anything else is a protocol violation. The reply also carries a write verifier, verf, which stays the same while the server runs and changes between server instances where uncommitted data may be lost.

If the verifier returned by COMMIT differs from the one the client saw earlier, the server may have lost the unsynchronized data, so the client must resend it. A server may also write fewer bytes than requested, and the client then issues another WRITE for the rest.
sections.eli5: Instead of walking each page to the archive room the moment you write it, you hand in a pile of pages and later ask, did all of those get filed? If the answer says the archive was restarted, you hand the pile in again.

sections.title: Retries and the Duplicate Request Cache
sections.content:
Failure recovery works by client time-out and retry. That is harmless for idempotent requests, which a server can perform more than once with equivalent results. It is dangerous for non-idempotent ones: a repeated CREATE can fail, and a file can be removed only once.

Most servers therefore keep a duplicate request cache: a short-term memory of recent requests and their original completion status. When a duplicate arrives, the server returns the original status instead of acting again. The RFC warns this is not a complete guarantee. Most servers keep the cache in RAM, so a crash loses it, and a network partition can cause an entry to be reused before the client gets its reply.

Servers must also be able to recover without data loss from multiple power failures, operating system failures and hardware failures other than the storage medium itself. Asynchronous writes also open a window for problems when clients share files: with no locking, the outcome of write sharing is indeterminate.
sections.eli5: If you ask the cafeteria for a sandwich twice because nobody answered, the cook checks a notepad of recent orders so you do not get two sandwiches. The notepad can get lost, so it is not perfect.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that sensitive file data may be sent or received, so authentication, privacy and data integrity should be addressed by implementations. As with version 2, NFS version 3 defers to the authentication provisions of the supporting RPC protocol (RFC 1057) and assumes that privacy and integrity come from the underlying transport layers where available.

The RFC describes four authentication flavors. AUTH_NONE passes no authentication information and is used for the NULL procedure. AUTH_UNIX sends the UNIX user ID, group ID and groups. AUTH_DES and AUTH_KERB use DES-encrypted parameters based on a network-wide name, with session keys from a public key scheme or Kerberos respectively. Client and server must agree on how users and groups map to identities.
sections.eli5: The server trusts the name tag you show at the door. Fancier name tags exist that are harder to fake, but locking the conversation itself is left to other layers.

messages.label: WRITE (UNSTABLE)
messages.note: Server may reply before data is on stable storage.

messages.label: WRITE reply: committed, verf
messages.note: The verifier identifies this server instance.

messages.label: COMMIT reply: verf
messages.note: A changed verifier means the data may be lost and must be resent.

items.label: UNSTABLE
items.desc: Server may commit any, all or none of the data before replying.

items.label: DATA_SYNC
items.desc: Data and enough metadata to retrieve it must be on stable storage.

items.label: FILE_SYNC
items.desc: Data and all file system metadata must be on stable storage, like version 2.
